sections.title: How does the Spherical coordinates calculator work?
sections.html:
The Spherical coordinates calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports r (Cartesian (x, y, z) to spherical (r, θ, φ)) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the x (Cartesian (x, y, z) to spherical (r, θ, φ)), the y (Cartesian (x, y, z) to spherical (r, θ, φ)), the z (Cartesian (x, y, z) to spherical (r, θ, φ)) and the r (Spherical (r, θ, φ) to Cartesian (x, y, z)).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

sections.title: The formula behind the Spherical coordinates calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

R=(the square root of ((X ^ 2) + (Y ^ 2) + (Z ^ 2)))
Φ=((Y, X))
Θ=((Z ÷ the square root of ((X ^ 2) + (Y ^ 2) + (Z ^ 2))))
X=(R × the sine of (Θ) × the cosine of (Φ))
Y=(R × the sine of (Φ) × the sine of (Θ))
Z=(R × the cosine of (Θ))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose x = 10, y = 10, z = 10 and r = 10. Working through the relationship above gives r = 17.3205, θ = 54.7356 deg, φ = 45 deg and x = 1.7101.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: r = 17.3205, θ = 54.7356 deg, φ = 45 deg and x = 1.7101 should be roughly the size you expected from x = 10 and y = 10.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Spherical coordinates calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a homework answer before you hand it in
  • Splitting a bill, a measurement or a shape problem between several people
  • Building the same calculation into a spreadsheet and wanting a reference value
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the x (Cartesian (x, y, z) to spherical (r, θ, φ)), the y (Cartesian (x, y, z) to spherical (r, θ, φ)) and the z (Cartesian (x, y, z) to spherical (r, θ, φ)) — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

faq.q: What does the Spherical coordinates calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns r (Cartesian (x, y, z) to spherical (r, θ, φ)). The inputs are listed in the article. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Spherical coordinates calculator?
faq.a: The form has 6 fields, each listed with its unit in the article above. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter θ (Cartesian (x, y, z) to spherical (r, θ, φ)) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Θ (Cartesian (x, y, z) to spherical (r, θ, φ)) opens in degrees and the chip beside it offers 12 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports r = 17.3205. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Spherical coordinates calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
